ABSTRACT
BACKGROUND Evidence regarding the benefits of catheter ablation in patients aged $80 years with nonvalvular
atrial fibrillation (AF) remains limited.
OBJECTIVES This study sought to evaluate the clinical effectiveness of catheter ablation compared with conservative
management in elderly patients (age $80 years) with nonvalvular AF.
METHODS This prospective, registry-based, multicenter observational study involved 703 patients aged $80 years
with nonvalvular AF enrolled from 47 hospitals in Japan (June 2022-December 2023). Among them, 249 underwent
catheter ablation and 454 received nonablation management.
RESULTS The nonablation group was slightly older, with more comorbidities and modestly worse baseline charac-
teristics; however, most were potential ablation candidates, and the differences were small. During a median follow-up
of 504 days (Q1-Q3: 375-667 days), the primary outcome (a composite of stroke, transient ischemic attack, systemic
embolism, cardiovascular events, bleeding, or all-cause death) did not differ between groups in the unmatched
(HR: 0.78; P = 0.30) or matched (HR: 0.65; P = 0.21) cohorts. However, in the matched cohort, multivariable
adjustment for log-N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide and albumin levels showed a significant benefit of ablation
(adjusted HR: 0.44; P = 0.029). At 1 year, ablation improved symptoms, quality of life, N-terminal pro–B-type
natriuretic peptide levels, and left atrial diameter, as well as better preservation of Mini–Mental State Examination and
frailty scores. These benefits remained significant after adjustment.

CONCLUSIONS The REHEALTH AF Study (Registry for Evaluating Healthy Life Expectancy and Long-Term
Outcomes After Catheter Ablation of Atrial Fibrillation in the Very Elderly) study is the first prospective
comparison of ablation vs nonablation in patients aged $80 years with AF. Although ablation improved
functional and structural outcomes, its prognostic benefit was limited without adjustment but emerged
after multivariable correction. Ablation may offer meaningful advantages in well-selected elderly patients,
supporting individualized treatment strategies. (Registry for Evaluating Healthy Life Expectancy and Long-Term
Outcomes After Catheter Ablation of Atrial Fibrillation in the Very Elderly [REHEALTH AF]; UMIN000047023)
(JACC Clin Electrophysiol. 2026;12:307–321) © 2026 by the American College of Cardiology Foundation.
A trial fibrillation (AF) increases the
risk of stroke, heart failure, and
mortality. 1-3 Early rhythm control
strategies, including catheter ablation, have
shown favorable clinical outcomes. 4-6 Over
the past 2 decades, advancements in ablation
technology have expanded its indications to
include not only younger patients but also
middle-aged and elderly patients. In Japan’s
“super-aged” society, AF ablation is now be-
ing increasingly applied to very elderly pa-
tients (ie, those aged $80 years). 7 Although
many studies have evaluated the efficacy and safety
of catheter ablation in elderly populations, most
have defined “elderly” as age $75 years. 8-10 As
such, evidence regarding the effects of ablation in pa-
tients aged $80 years remains limited, despite this
subgroup facing unique clinical challenges. 11-14
Importantly, randomized controlled trials such as
the CABANA (Catheter Ablation Versus Antiar-
rhythmic Drug Therapy for Atrial Fibrillation) and
the CASTLE-AF (Catheter Ablation for Atrial Fibrilla-
tion with Heart Failure) trials have not shown a sig-
nificant prognostic benefit of catheter ablation in
older adults, particularly for hard outcomes such as
mortality or stroke.
These findings underscore the need for further
investigation into the true value of ablation in the
very elderly, beyond traditional endpoints. Further-
more, no previous studies have comprehensively

evaluated the trajectory of the quality of life (QoL),
physical and mental function, or laboratory parame-
ters such as hemoglobin or renal function over time
in patients aged $80 years after ablation. To address
these critical knowledge gaps, we conducted the
REHEALTH AF (Registry for Evaluating Healthy Life
Expectancy and Long-Term Outcomes After Catheter
Ablation of Atrial Fibrillation in the Very Elderly)
study, a multicenter, prospective, observational
registry. This study aimed to assess the effects of
catheter ablation on the QoL, physical and mental
status, and clinical outcomes in patients aged $80
years, while also capturing real-world longitudinal
data in patients who underwent ablation and those
who did not.
METHODS
STUDY DESIGN AND SETTING. The REHEALTH AF
study is a large-scale, multicenter, prospective reg-
istry of patients with AF in Japan. Patient enrollment
began on June 1, 2022, and ended on December 31,
2023. All enrolled patients were followed up for at
least 1 year, with the final follow-up scheduled on or
before December 31, 2024. A total of 47 hospitals
across Japan are participating in the registry
(Supplemental Figure 1), comprising 35 ablation-
performing centers and 12 centers where ablation is
not performed. The study design and protocol of the
REHEALTH AF study have been published
previously. 15
ELIGIBILITY AND EXCLUSION CRITERIA. Patients
aged $80 years with nonvalvular AF were eligible. All
were outpatients who elected either ablation or
nonablation management based on physician
recommendation or personal preference. The study
included all AF types: paroxysmal (spontaneously
terminating within 7 days), persistent (>7 days),
long-standing persistent (>1 year), and permanent
(not amenable to cardioversion). To ensure
comparability, the nonablation group was prospec-
tively restricted to relatively healthy candidates
considered suitable for ablation. This approach
enhanced the quality of subsequent propensity score
matching while preserving the advantages of pro-
spective enrollment.
Exclusion criteria included prior ablation within
12 months, a Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) score $7, 16
severe dementia, severe valvular disease, active
malignancy, ongoing hemodialysis, or other condi-
tions deemed unsuitable by investigators. Of 714
enrolled patients, 11 were excluded (2 withdrawal of
consent, 9 loss to follow-up), yielding 703 patients
(249 ablation, 454 nonablation) (Figure 1).
STUDY SCHEDULE. The design and study procedures
of the REHEALTH AF study have been published
previously. 15 In brief, baseline evaluations included
clinical characteristics, laboratory tests, echocardio-
gram, frailty (CFS), 16 and QoL (five-level European
Quality of Life-5 Dimensions [EQ-5D-5L] index and
visual analog scale). An optional cognitive assess-
ment was performed by using the Mini–Mental State
Examination (MMSE).
Patients who elected to undergo catheter ablation
were evaluated within 1 month before the procedure.
Patients in the ablation group underwent catheter
ablation for AF, followed by routine outpatient
follow-up, which included regular clinic visits, elec-
trocardiogram monitoring, and medical management
as per clinical judgment. In the nonablation group,
management strategies were predominantly based on
rate control, with rhythm control applied in selected
cases, at the discretion of the treating physician.
Follow-up assessments at 12 months were per-
formed in the majority of patients, including those in
the nonablation group, where data on the CFS,
symptoms, QoL, and clinical parameters were avail-
able. Clinical endpoints, medication changes, and
procedural interventions were collected in both
groups, while any episode of recurrent AF or atrial

tachyarrhythmia (AT) in the ablation group (lasting
>30 seconds and documented by a standard electro-
cardiogram, event recorder, or 24-hour Holter
monitoring) was also assessed every 3 to 6 months
during follow-up. If patients were followed up for
>1.5 years, an additional assessment was optionally
scheduled.
All data were pseudonymized and entered into a
secure web-based registry system by trained site
personnel. The registry was centrally monitored, and
a clinical event committee adjudicated the end-
points. The full study schedule is summarized in the
previously published design paper 15 and in
Supplemental Table 1.
PRIMARY AND SECONDARY ENDPOINTS. The pri-
mary study endpoint was the composite incidence of
stroke/transient ischemic attack (TIA) or systemic
embolism, other cardiovascular events (excluding
stroke/TIA/systemic embolism and cardiovascular
death), clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding and
major bleeding (CRNMB/MB), and/or all-cause death.
MB was defined according to the International Soci-
ety on Thrombosis and Haemostasis criteria as fatal
bleeding, symptomatic bleeding in a critical area or
organ (eg, intracranial, intraspinal, intraocular, peri-
cardial, retroperitoneal), a hemoglobin decrease
$20 g/L, or transfusion of $2 units of blood. 17
CRNMB was defined as bleeding that did not meet the

criteria for MB but required medical intervention,
unscheduled contact with a physician, interruption
of anticoagulant therapy, or led to increased level of
care. In the ablation group, treatment-related com-
plications such as cardiac tamponade, vascular com-
plications requiring surgery, stroke-TIA, and other
cardiovascular events were included as components
of the primary composite endpoint. Procedural safety
was monitored systematically throughout the study
period. Key secondary endpoints included stroke/
TIA/systemic embolism, heart failure requiring hos-
pitalization, other cardiovascular events, CRNMB/
MB, and all-cause death (cardiovascular death and
non-cardiovascular death). A full list of primary and
secondary endpoints is presented in Supplemental
Table 2.
Also evaluated were the changes from baseline to
1 year in the CFS score, EQ-5D-5L index score, MMSE
score (optional), Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index
(GNRI), N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide
(NT-proBNP) levels, and left atrial diameter (LAD) as
indicators of functional, cognitive, and structural
outcomes. The GNRI, a validated nutritional index
predictive of morbidity and mortality in elderly
populations, 18 was used to assess the nutritional
status. Additional follow-up assessments are listed in
Supplemental Table 2.
STATISTICAL ANALYSIS. Continuous variables are
presented as mean ± SD or median (Q1-Q3) and cat-
egorical variables as counts and percentages.
Between-group differences were assessed by using
the Student’s t-test or Mann-Whitney U test for
continuous variables, and the chi-square or Fisher
exact test for categorical variables. Event rates were
summarized as counts, percentages, and incidence
per 100 person-years. Crude Cox proportional haz-
ards models and Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard
models were used to estimate the effect of catheter
ablation on clinical outcomes. Results are presented
as HRs or subdistribution HRs (SHRs) with corre-
sponding 95% CIs. These analyses were applied to all
secondary endpoints.
For heart failure hospitalizations, in which
all-cause death was considered a competing risk,
cumulative incidence functions were calculated and
compared by using Gray’s test. SHRs with 95% CIs
were derived in both the overall and matched
cohorts.
To address baseline imbalances, 1:1 nearest-
neighbor propensity score matching was performed
with a caliper width of 0.2. In sensitivity analyses,
inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW)
was performed by using propensity scores from a
prespecified logistic model including key baseline
covariates. Stabilized weights were applied, and the
covariate balance was evaluated by standardized
mean differences (target <0.10) (Figure 1). 19 Kaplan-
Meier curves and log-rank tests were used to
compare the cumulative incidence of the primary
outcome in both the overall and matched cohorts.
Finally, a multivariable Cox model was constructed
in the matched cohort to identify independent pre-
dictors of the primary outcome, yielding adjusted
HRs with 95% CIs. Subgroup analyses were con-
ducted by using Cox proportional hazards models
stratified according to age, sex, body mass index, AF
type, frailty, renal function, NT-proBNP level, and
LAD subgroups. Within each subgroup, adjusted HRs
and interaction P values were calculated by using
models that included relevant covariates tailored to
each subgroup (Supplemental Table 3).
As additional exploratory analyses, outcomes were
compared within the ablation group (radiofrequency
vs balloon energy, nonparoxysmal AF vs paroxysmal
AF, and recurrence vs non-recurrence) and within the
nonablation group (rhythm vs rate control), between
the nonablation and ablation groups (rhythm vs
ablation, rate vs ablation). These results are shown in
Supplemental Figures 2 and 3. For clinical parameters
assessed at baseline and at 1 year (eg, symptoms,
CFS, EQ-5D-5L, MMSE, GNRI, NT-proBNP, LAD),
within-group changes were evaluated by using paired
Student t-tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, or
McNemar’s test as appropriate. Between-group dif-
ferences in changes were assessed by using unpaired
Student t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests, followed by
linear regression (least squares) or a quantile
regression adjusted for relevant covariates. For the
binary symptom status (eg, presence or absence of
any AF-related symptom), changes in asymptomatic
proportions between groups were further analyzed
by using multivariable logistic regression models
adjusting for the same 14 baseline covariates used in
the propensity score model. Multiplicity was not
accounted for, as all analyses were exploratory in
nature.
A 2-sided P value <0.05 was considered statisti-
cally significant. All statistical analyses were per-
formed by using JMP Pro 17 or SAS 9.4 (SAS Institute,
Inc).
ETHICS APPROVAL AND DISSEMINATION. The study
was approved by the Institutional Review Board of
Nihon University Itabashi Hospital (Institutional
Review Board no. RK-220412-9) and all participating
centers. It was conducted in accordance with the

RESULTS
BASELINE CHARACTERISTICS. The patient charac-
teristics are summarized in Table 1. Compared with the
ablation group, the nonablation group was signifi-
cantly older, had a higher prevalence of long-standing
persistent AF, higher CFS scores, more comorbidities,
higher risk scores (CHADS 2 , CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc, and HAS-
BLED scores), lower creatinine clearance, smaller
LAD, and less frequent antiarrhythmic drug use.
However, because patients in the nonablation group
were prospectively enrolled from among those
considered potential candidates for ablation, the
observed differences, although statistically signifi-
cant in some variables, were not extreme overall.
PRIMARY AND SECONDARY ENDPOINTS. O v e r a l l
O u t c o m e s . The median follow-up was 504 days
(Q1-Q3: 375-667 days). The primary composite
endpoint occurred in 24 patients (9.6% [6.8% per
year]) in the ablation group and 56 patients (12.4%
[8.7% per year]) in the nonablation group (HR: 0.78;
95% CI: 0.48-1.25; log-rank test, P = 0.30) (Figure 2A,
Table 2). Secondary endpoints showed no significant
differences, including heart failure hospitalizations
(4.4% vs 6.2%; Gray’s test, P = 0.30), all-cause death
(0.8% vs 2.4%; P = 0.13), or individual components
such as stroke/TIA/systemic embolism, bleeding, or
other cardiovascular events (Figures 2B and 2C,
Table 2).
A d j u s t e d A n a l y s e s . The matched analysis yielded
results consistent with the overall cohort. The pri-
mary composite endpoint (7.3% [5.1% per year] vs
10.9% [7.9% per year]; HR: 0.65; 95% CI: 0.33-1.27;
log-rank test, P = 0.20) (Figure 2D). After multivari-
able adjustment for albumin and log-NT-proBNP
levels, the primary composite endpoint was signifi-
cantly reduced with ablation (adjusted HR: 0.44;
95% CI: 0.21-0.92; P = 0.029) (Central Illustration).
However, IPTW analysis showed no significant dif-
ference (HR: 0.97; 95% CI: 0.70-1.34) (Supplemental
Table 4), consistent with the overall and propensity
score–matched analyses. Similarly, Kaplan-Meier
curves for heart failure hospitalizations (Figure 2E)
and all-cause death (Figure 2F) were not statistically
significant. Notably, the incidence of CRNMB/MB was
lower in the ablation group (0.5% vs 4.2%; HR: 0.12;
95% CI: 0.02-0.99; P = 0.049) (Table 2).

S u b g r o u p s . No interaction by age, sex, body mass
index, AF type, frailty, renal function, NT-proBNP, or
LAD was observed (Figure 3). Patients with a CFS
score >3 showed a trend toward greater benefit
(adjusted HR: 0.30; 95% CI: 0.13-0.90; P = 0.030;
P interaction = 0.064).
P r o c e d u r a l S a f e t y . In the ablation group, major
periprocedural events included 2 cardiac tamponades
(1 with radiofrequency [0.6%], 1 with cryoballoon
[1.2%]), 1 stroke/TIA (0.6%; radiofrequency), and 2
vascular complications (1.2%; both radiofrequency).
Event rates did not differ significantly between
radiofrequency and balloon energy (2.4% vs 1.2%;
P = 1.0).
E x p l o r a t o r y A n a l y s e s . In the ablation cohort, the
primary composite outcome occurred in 11.4% with
radiofrequency vs 6.1% with balloon energy (HR:
1.84; 95% CI: 0.69-4.93; P = 0.23). Outcomes were
also similar between non-paroxysmal and parox-
ysmal AF (11.7% vs 8.2%; HR: 1.47; 95% CI: 0.66-3.28;
P = 0.34). During follow-up, AF/AT recurrence
occurred in 29 patients (11.6%) and was associated
with a higher risk of the primary outcome (24.1% vs
7.7%; HR: 3.45; 95% CI: 1.43-8.32; P < 0.05)
(Supplemental Figure 2). In the nonablation group,
rhythm control vs rate control strategies showed no
difference (HR: 1.04; 95% CI: 0.57-1.92; P = 0.88),
with pairwise comparisons also nonsignificant
(Supplemental Figure 3).
CHANGES IN THE PARAMETERS. AF-related symp-
toms, including palpitations, dizziness, rapid heart-
beat, dyspnea, and syncope, but not fatigue, were
more frequent at baseline in the ablation group but
improved markedly after ablation. The proportion of
asymptomatic patients increased by 42.3% with
ablation vs 13.3% with nonablation, resulting in
similar proportions at 1 year (57.7% vs 56.8%;
P = 0.82; adjusted P = 0.13) (Figure 4).
As summarized in Table 3 and Supplemental
Table 5, ablation led to significant improvements
in QoL (EQ-5D-5L index and VAS, both P < 0.001
within group; adjusted between group, P = 0.032
and < 0.001), preservation of cognitive function
(MMSE stable vs decline; adjusted P = 0.008), and
stable frailty status (CFS stable vs worsening;

DISCUSSION
The main findings of this study were as follows:
during approximately 1.5 years of follow-up, there
were no significant differences in primary composite
clinical events between the ablation and nonablation
groups after propensity score matching. However,
multivariate Cox regression showed a significantly
lower risk of the composite outcome in the ablation
group. Notably, ablation provided substantial bene-
fits in symptoms, QoL, and preservation of physical
and cognitive function.
Our findings align with subgroup analyses from
CABANA, 20 CASTLE AF, 13 and EAST-AFNET 4 (Early
Treatment of Atrial Fibrillation for Stroke Prevention
Trial), 4 which showed limited prognostic benefit in
older patients. However, no prior studies have
focused exclusively on the population aged $80
years, making our findings particularly relevant to
this growing demographic. In very elderly patients,
competing risks from comorbidities such as frailty,
renal dysfunction, and anemia may outweigh the
impact of AF itself on prognosis. Nevertheless, after
adjustment for NT-proBNP and albumin levels,
ablation was associated with lower risk of adverse
events, suggesting a potential benefit in carefully
selected patients. Interestingly, a subgroup analysis
showed that patients with a higher CFS score (>3)
benefited significantly from catheter ablation after
adjustment. One possibility is that frail patients are
more vulnerable to the hemodynamic effects of AF,
and maintaining sinus rhythm may offer them
greater symptomatic and prognostic improvements.
Alternatively, selection bias may have contributed,
as patients too frail for ablation were likely excluded.
Given the limited sample size, this finding should be
interpreted cautiously and regarded as hypothesis-
generating.
Importantly, functional and patient-centered out-
comes improved. Ablation resulted in better symp-
tom relief, improved QoL, decreased NT-proBNP
levels, and reduced LAD, whereas nonablation pa-
tients showed minimal improvement or decline. The
CABANA trial likewise reported symptoms and QoL
benefits even in patients aged $75 years, 14 and a
recent US registry also reported QoL improvements
in older ablation patients (age $75 years). 21 These
suggest consistency; however, confirmation in $80-

catheter ablation resulted in better 1-year symptoms, QoL, NT-proBNP, and LAD, with

for baseline characteristics revealed a statistically
significant between-group difference (adjusted
P < 0.001), suggesting subtle but consistent shifts in
the frailty distribution. The between-group differ-
ence in LAD change was also small and within the
range of reported echocardiographic measurement
variability; however, we interpret LAD change as
supportive evidence in the context of concordant
improvements in NT-proBNP, symptoms, QoL,
frailty, and cognition, rather than as a stand-alone
marker of remodeling. Notably, cognitive function,
assessed by the MMSE, was preserved in the ablation
group but declined in the nonablation group. This
finding suggests that maintaining sinus rhythm may
help prevent a cognitive decline, an important
finding, as recent studies link AF to cerebral hypo-
perfusion and an increased risk of dementia. 22-24 The
observed benefits for symptoms, biomarkers, and
cognitive function may reflect improved hemody-
namics from restored atrial contraction and regular
ventricular response, helping preserve frailty status.
In this context, preservation of the physical and
cognitive function may represent an important
extension of a healthy life expectancy in elderly pa-
tients undergoing ablation. Although recurrence
rates may be higher in older patients due to advanced
atrial remodeling, 25 even partial rhythm control can
yield functional benefits. Nevertheless, procedural

risk 26 and frailty must be weighed against physio-
logical reserve. In the current study, ablated patients
were relatively healthy octogenarians. Within the
ablation group, outcomes did not differ significantly
by energy source (radiofrequency vs balloon) or AF
type (non-paroxysmal vs paroxysmal AF) but recur-
rence was strongly associated with worse outcomes;
this underscores the importance of careful pre-
procedural assessment to determine whether abla-
tion should be avoided rather than simply
minimizing recurrence in frail patients or those with
high-risk substrates.
STUDY STRENGTHS AND DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS.
First, conducting an randomized controlled trial in
this population is ethically and practically chal-
lenging: we therefore adopted a prospective, multi-
center observational design that allowed for broad
enrollment across 47 sites in Japan and reflected
real-world clinical practice. Importantly, we delib-
erately included both ablation-performing and
nonablation centers, thereby enrolling ablation-
eligible patients irrespective of referral patterns,
which helped reduce potential selection bias. Sec-
ond, because patients who undergo ablation tend to
be healthier than those who do not, 11 we prospec-
tively enrolled nonablation patients who were
considered clinically eligible for ablation. This
allowed us to evaluate not only clinical outcomes
but also symptoms, frailty, cognition, and QoL,
endpoints especially relevant in the very elderly.
Third, rhythm control therapies were infrequently
used in the nonablation group, mirroring routine
practice and enhancing generalizability.
CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS. In octogenarians with AF,
catheter ablation may not necessarily reduce the
incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events,
but it can provide meaningful benefits in terms of
symptom relief, QoL, preservation of physical and
cognitive function, and reverse cardiac remodeling.
In contrast, rate and rhythm control strategies yiel-
ded similar primary composite outcomes in the
nonablation group, underscoring that ablation may
represent the only intervention with potential
modest clinical outcome advantages in this popula-
tion, provided that patients are carefully selected.
Clinical decision-making should therefore emphasize
frailty status, comorbidities, and personal goals of
care, rather than relying solely on age or rhythm
control efficacy. Given the modest impact on hard
events but consistent gains in symptoms, QoL,
frailty, and cognition, future studies in octogenarians
should consider disability-free survival or related
patient-centered composites (eg, independence,
institutionalization, cognitive preservation, quality-
adjusted life years) as primary or co-primary
endpoints.

STUDY LIMITATIONS. First, as an observational
study, even with matching and IPTW, causality
cannot be established. Residual or unmeasured con-
founding and selection bias, including treatment
assignment by physician or patient preference,
cannot be fully excluded, inevitably limiting causal
inference compared with randomized controlled tri-
als such as CABANA 20 or CASTLE AF. 13 Second,
because all participants were aged $80 years, we
used relatively simple patient-reported outcomes for
symptoms and QoL, which may not fully capture all
aspects of the AF-related functional status. Third, the
MMSE was assessed as an optional item, and the
subset of patients who underwent MMSE testing
showed distinct baseline characteristics, including
higher prevalence of stroke history, device therapy,
cancer, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease,
as well as higher left ventricular ejection fraction and
albumin levels (data are not shown), which may have
introduced selection bias and limited the generaliz-
ability of cognitive findings. Fourth, although we
acknowledge that neither the CFS nor the GNRI has
been validated exclusively in $80-year-old AF abla-
tion cohorts, both indices have been widely used and
validated in AF and elderly populations; this includes
studies linking CFS to anticoagulation patterns and
outcomes in elderly patients with AF 27 and GNRI to
arrhythmia recurrence or mortality in AF co-
horts. 28,29 These prior validations justify their use in
the current study. Fifth, the study population con-
sisted entirely of Japanese patients. Japan’s super-
aged demographic structure and health care system
differ from those in other regions, and thus extrap-
olation beyond Japan should be done with caution.
Multinational studies are warranted to confirm
applicability. Sixth, procedural heterogeneity may
exist: operator experience, procedural volume
(although most procedures were conducted in high-
volume centers by experienced electrophysiolo-
gists), and rhythm-monitoring intensity were not
strictly standardized, potentially introducing detec-
tion bias in arrhythmia recurrence. Finally, within
the nonablation group, some heterogeneity in man-
agement (rhythm vs rate control) may have
remained, although subgroup analyses showed no
significant differences in outcomes. Despite these
limitations, this is the first large-scale, prospective
study specifically designed to compare ablation and
nonablation therapy in very elderly patients with AF.
CONCLUSIONS
The REHEALTH AF study is the first prospective,
multicenter observational study to evaluate the
impact of catheter ablation in patients aged $80
years with nonvalvular AF. Although ablation did not
reduce major adverse events or mortality, it signifi-
cantly improved symptoms, quality of life, and
markers of physical and cognitive function. These
findings highlight the importance of individualized
treatment strategies that carefully weigh procedural
risks against the potential benefits of preserving

PERSPECTIVES
COMPETENCY IN PATIENT CARE AND
PROCEDURAL SKILLS: In very elderly patients
(age $80 years) with AF, catheter ablation was
feasible and associated with meaningful improve-
ments in symptoms, QoL, cognitive function, and
cardiac remodeling. However, its impact on the
composite primary clinical outcomes was limited.
Treatment decisions should be individualized by
integrating frailty, comorbidities, and patient prefer-
ences, while also considering health care resources
and system-level factors. The therapeutic value of
ablation in this population may lie more in functional
and QoL preservation than in prognostic benefit, and
its adoption should be interpreted in the context of
cost-effectiveness and health care priorities across
different regions worldwide.
TRANSLATIONAL OUTLOOK: Future studies
should aim to reduce selection bias through pro-
spective, ideally randomized, comparative designs in
diverse elderly populations. Extended follow-up
focusing on functional and cognitive outcomes will be
essential to clarify whether ablation contributes to
preserving independence and healthy life expectancy
in very elderly patients.
